newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Japanese rates said to start rising in q3 or q4.
newsitem.headline: Japanese rates said to start rising in q3 or q4.

text.p: The Bank of Japan will probably start to raise interest rates incrementally in the third or fourth quarter of 1997, said the president of Japan's Institute for International Monetary Affairs Toyoo Gyohten.

"We had considerable fiscal drag imposed in April and I think the real impact of that fiscal drag on the economic recovery will be clear by the end of the second quarter," he told reporters at the International Management Symposium.
"So I think at the earliest (interest rates will rise) during the third quarter and quite likely during the fourth quarter. That is my guess.
"They will probably follow an incremental approach, not very drastic ones."

Gyohten, senior adviser to the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd and a former official of the Ministry of Finace, and said he thought the Japanese economy would grow between two and 2.5 percent in calendar 1997.
Growth was not robust enough to justify drastic monetary tightening.
Gyohten thought the yen had settled into a realistic range of between 110 and 120 to the dollar.
"Personally I think that, at today's rate of 116, it is still on the weak side. I personally would like to see a bit stronger yen," he said.

"But if the yen remains within the range of 110 to 120, I think everybody will be not too unhappy and that is very important," he said, adding that range would not create "serious discomfort" for either Japanese or U.S. policymakers.
Markets are increasingly sensitive to potential interest rate rise in the United States and Japan and to Japan's bilateral current account surplus, Gyohten said.
"I think Japan's surplus will continue to grow because we are now in the period of the delayed impact of the weaker yen since the spring of 1995. This increase will stay with us for some time."

He expected currency markets to remain volatile, but added he hoped the experience of the past couple years had persusaded officials of the need for cooprative action to prevent overshooting of exchange rates.
Verbal intervention by Japanese officials talking up the yen succeeded because markets were already jittery about the dollar.
